4.text: I am not aware of a pump-drill being used for making fire by the Chuk-

5.text: chee, as is stated by W. Hough.¹ The fire-drill board for every-day use
5.note: Footnote 1 reference, superscript per keying_spec.md §2.10 (machine draft substituted '!' for the raised digit, a known CATMuS failure mode).

6.text: sometimes has no particular shape, the real gɪˊrgɪr being kept for ceremonials.
6.resolved: gɪˊrgɪr = g, ɪ(U+026A), U+02CA, r, g, ɪ(U+026A), r
6.note: Same form as line 2, reconfirmed at 4x.

7.text: The board and the drill are usually made of the same wood, on the Arctic

8.text: coast more frequently of Canadian pine, which is found everywhere along the

9.text: shore in the driftwood. In the interior they are made of poplar and aspen.

10.text: To work successfully, both parts must be completely dry. Therefore in damp

11.text: weather the Chukchee women sometimes have considerable trouble in obtaining

13.text: The board has several rows of holes, marked at first with a knife, and

14.text: then made deeper by means of the drill. The upper piece is almost always

15.text: made of the astragalus of a reindeer, while the Koryak use also wood and

16.text: stone. It is held in position with the left hand or with the breast. The board

17.text: is kept in place with the foot, while the right hand moves the bow, the

18.text: string of which winds around the drill (see Plate XIX, Fig. 3 opp. p. 198).
18.note: Plate XIX set in small-cap typography in print; roman numerals keyed plain ASCII capitals per keying_spec.md §2.12.

19.text: Too hard pressure on the top of the drill makes the process slower.

20.text: While turning in the hole, the drill produces a shrill sound, which is regarded

21.text: as the voice of the gɪˊrgɪr.
21.resolved: gɪˊrgɪr = g, ɪ(U+026A), U+02CA, r, g, ɪ(U+026A), r
21.note: Same form as lines 2 and 6, reconfirmed at 4x.

22.text: When the wood is dry, smoke begins to rise out of the hole after a few

23.text: seconds. To produce a flame, however, requires considerable skill. Often to

24.text: increase the friction, a little coal is put into the hole under the drill. The

25.text: lighting of the spark is indicated by a rapid increase in the density of smoke,

26.text: not unlike the steam from boiling water. Then the drill is laid aside, and

27.text: the board gently swung in the air to keep the spark alive. After that a

28.text: minute portion of burning charcoal is quickly taken out of the board and put

29.text: among some dry coals; and the fire is rapidly kindled by swinging it about

30.text: and blowing it, at the same time feeding it with little chips and splinters of

31.text: dry wood. The whole process, when the operator is experienced, requires not

32.text: more than five minutes. The fire-drill, together with the chips and coals

33.text: necessary for the process, is always kept carefully wrapped in dry skins and

34.text: hidden in the depths of some voluminous bag to preserve it from dampness.

35.text: At present the fire-tools in most common use are the flint and steel (Fig.

36.text: 167, a). They are bought from the Russians or the Lamut, who, while wandering

37.text: across large territories, usually take the trouble to find the best pieces of flint,

38.text: and to keep them for barter with the Chukchee. The touch-wood is made

39.text: of a kind of fungus which is found on the poplar and aspen. This is the

40.text: same as that used by the Alaskan Eskimo, and represented by Nelson.² The
